study.comments: Table 1 reports only percentages per species and agent; the header does not state the category, but the text interprets them as resistance (C. tropicalis 100% resistant to fluconazole and itraconazole). Counts calculated from % with n=15. Resistance rates near 100% for almost all agents across all species (including amphotericin B 60% and nystatin 93%) are implausible and suggest methodological problems (disc diffusion with non-standard criteria for several agents, e.g. nystatin/clotrimazole have no CLSI breakpoints). The C. tropicalis ATCC 10610 control strain is not a field isolate. No MICs.

study.comments: Only non-albicans Candida (1000 NAC isolates). Table 1 lists 9 hospital columns while text says 10 hospitals. Serious internal inconsistencies for C. tropicalis: text says only 4.3% susceptible to fluconazole and 3.9% to posaconazole, but Table 2 gives FLC MIC50 2 µg/mL (≤2 = S under M60, implying ≥50% S) and POS MIC50 0.031 µg/mL; anidulafungin MIC50 (0.016) below the reported range minimum (0.0312). Categorical counts calculated from % and therefore uncertain. Abstract also states 10% of all isolates susceptible to caspofungin, inconsistent with low CAS MICs.

clade4.evidence: this eBURST group of the four azoles resistant isolates also included the resistant isolates from Taiwan and China identified previously (Chou et al., 2007; Fan et al., 2017). This implied that this eBURST group 3 is strongly associated with the triazole resistance of Asian C. tropicalis isolates.
clade4.note: Authors call it 'eBURST group 3'; equivalence with the clade 4 / azole-resistant cluster of other studies is inferred from the stated inclusion of the Taiwanese and Chinese resistant isolates. 'Azole resistant' = resistant/non-WT to all four triazoles. Specific DSTs of group 3 are not given in the text (figure only). p < 0.001 for association.

dynamics.description: Proportion of C. tropicalis among candidaemia at Siriraj Hospital rose from 28.0% (2006-2009, Boonyasiri et al. 2013) to 46.7% (2012-2018; 2,048 Candida blood isolates).
Fluconazole resistance in Thai C. tropicalis rose from 0% (1999-2002, Foongladda et al. 2004, cited) to 43.8% in this study (2015-2017).
